content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Describe the properties of noble gases
Explain why noble gases are unreactive
Explain the uses of noble gases
(Group 0 or Group 8/18) are helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon, and radon. They are colourless, odourless gases that are remarkably unreactive - so unreactive they were once called "inert gases."
All noble gases have full outer electron shells:
They don't need to gain, lose, or share electrons
They don't form ions or covalent bonds (usually)
They don't react with other elements
Boiling point INCREASES down the group
Atoms get larger down the group
More electrons = stronger London dispersion forces (van der Waals)
More energy needed to separate atoms
Light bulbs (inert atmosphere prevents filament burning)
Can accumulate in buildings - must be monitored
Explain why argon is used in light bulbs instead of air.
At high temperatures, oxygen would react with the metal filament
The filament would oxidise and burn out quickly
It won't react with the hot filament
Explain why noble gases are unreactive in terms of their electronic configuration.
Noble gases have full outer electron shells
Other noble gases have 8 electrons in their outer shell
A full outer shell is a very stable arrangement
There is no need to lose, gain, or share electrons
Chemical reactions involve electron transfer or sharing
Since noble gases don't need to do this, they don't react
They are chemically stable as single atoms
Explain the trend in boiling points of noble gases.
Boiling points increase down the group
Noble gas atoms get larger going down the group
More electrons means stronger van der Waals (London dispersion) forces between atoms
More energy is needed to overcome these stronger forces
He has the lowest boiling point (-269°C); Rn has the highest (-62°C)
Why is helium used in airships instead of hydrogen?
Both helium and hydrogen are lighter than air (can lift airships)
Hydrogen is flammable and can explode (Hindenburg disaster)
Helium is non-flammable because it's a noble gas
Helium won't react with oxygen even with a spark
Helium provides nearly the same lifting power but with no fire risk
Thinking noble gases have 0 outer electrons
Group 0 means FULL outer shell (8 electrons, or 2 for He)
Writing noble gases as molecules (e.g., He₂)
Noble gases are monatomic - they exist as single atoms
They are very unreactive, but heavy ones (Xe) can form some compounds
State three properties of noble gases. (3 marks)
Explain why noble gases are unreactive, referring to their electronic configuration. (3 marks)
Describe and explain the trend in boiling points of noble gases going down Group 0. (4 marks)

Why are noble gases described as 'monatomic'? (2 marks)
Helium is used in balloons instead of hydrogen. Explain why. (3 marks)
A Group 0 element with a full outer electron shell
Existing as single atoms, not molecules
Having the maximum number of electrons in the outer shell
= Noble gases: He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn
Ar: light bulbs, welding, double glazing
